svg.title: Urban Analytics Lab lecture poster — 2 speakers

text.tspan: Estimating Building Style, Quality and Performance with
Multi-source Ground Sensing Data in Mustang, Nepal
This study presents a multi-dimensional, settlement-level assessment of the built environment
in Mustang, Nepal, using multi-source ground-sensing data and Multimodal Large Language
Models (MLLMs). Mustang, a high-altitude Tibetan-Buddhist cultural landscape, is undergoing
rapid transformation due to tourism, road construction, and climate stress, yet systematic,
building-level data across its settlements remain scarce. To address this gap, we curated 6,495
geo-tagged images from three sources—field photography, vehicle-mounted GoPro video, and
Google Street View—covering 45 settlements and 9,314 building footprints. Using a fine-tuned
MLLM, we evaluated each building along three dimensions: Tibetan architectural style
(perception score and 17 element flags), physical quality (1–5 scale), and use-performance
(occupancy status, 1–4 scale). Results reveal a sharp north-south gradient in style, driven by
building-body features rather than ornament; a negative correlation between traditional
character and maintenance, indicating an authenticity-vulnerability trade-off; and a strong
positive link between physical quality and active use. This work contributes a reproducible,
low-cost pipeline for vernacular landscape assessment and offers empirical evidence for
prioritizing living building heritage in conservation policy.

g.inkscape:label: Speaker 2

text.tspan: From Human Mobility Data to Spatial Intelligence for
Inclusive and Sustainable Cities

g.text: Professor Chen Zhong, University College London

text.tspan: Emerging data sources, spatial intelligence, and interdisciplinary perspectives have
continually pushed the boundaries of urban analytics, expanding what we can observe,
understand and model urban systems. The notion of boundaries lies at the heart of this
progress—both as a conceptual lens and as an empirical reality. Cities are shaped by physical,
administrative, and social boundaries that influence human mobility, spatial interactions, and
patterns of inequality, while advances in human mobility data, GeoAI, and computational
methods continue to redefine the boundaries of what can be measured and understood. This
presentation will reflect on the evolution of human mobility data, spatial analytics, and GeoAI,
highlighting how these advances have deepened our understanding of spatial structures and
urban dynamics while enhancing our capacity for data- and model-informed digital planning.
Drawing on the team’s recent research progress on socio-spatial inequality in activity space,
we will conclude with an overview of our research agenda on urban mobility data and GeoAI
methods for inclusive and sustainable mobility planning.
